claims.text: Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is a dual-nanoprecipitation high-entropy alloy.
The Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is produced via additive manufacturing.
High-temperature oxidation causes measurable elemental redistribution at nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces in this alloy.
Atom Probe Tomography can elucidate oxidation-induced elemental redistribution at nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces.
The initial microstructure contains nanoscale dispersed precipitates within a solid-solution matrix.
The alloy will be exposed to high-temperature oxidation representative of gas-turbine, power-plant, or aerospace environments.
Controlled oxidation at approximately 1000–1100 °C can be used to simulate service conditions.
Nanoprecipitates and their interfaces mediate oxidation behavior through compositional and structural changes.
High-temperature oxidation drives diffusion of Al, Ti, and Cr in this alloy.
Oxidation-driven diffusion causes elemental segregation at nanoprecipitate interfaces.
Oxide phases form at nanoprecipitate interfaces during high-temperature oxidation.
APT provides near-atomic-resolution three-dimensional mapping of subtle compositional gradients and redistribution.
Oxidized samples will show statistically significant elemental gradients and segregation at nanoprecipitate interfaces relative to an unoxidized baseline.
Unoxidized AM-processed samples can provide a baseline for nanoprecipitate composition and distribution measured by APT.
Temperature, oxidation duration, and alloy processing may affect the magnitude and character of elemental redistribution.
The exact magnitude of redistribution and its quantitative relationship to oxidation resistance are unknown until experimentally measured.
Failure to detect statistically significant or consistent interfacial redistribution relative to the unoxidized baseline would falsify the proposed detectable-redistribution hypothesis.
